title: Judge points out police info gaps
article: An inquiry into the 2003 fatal shooting of a Sudanese immigrant points to the need for the Calgary Police Service to step up communication and information available to officers responding to potentially violent calls.

Four out of the five recommendations by fatality inquiry judge Gerald Meagher point to communication breakdowns the night Const. Ira Macumber responded to a disturbance call in a southeast Calgary apartment hallway.
While some members of the Sudanese community still have concerns, the lawyer for Deng Fermino Kuol's family accepts the findings.
Police Chief Jack Beaton said Tuesday all the recommendations have either been implemented or are in the process of being addressed.
Beaton admitted the current information management system was first built more than 20 years ago.
He would like to have a provincewide system to link all police databases that communications officers could access to provide information to officers on the street.
Beaton said this would come with a hefty price tag, likely in the $100-200 million range, and would require funding from the province.
"It's time to make a plan to move ahead with a good record management system that allows us to exchange data," Beaton said.
On Oct. 25, 2003, police were called to a Forest Lawn apartment to ask a drunken, knife-wielding Kuol to leave the property, the inquiry heard.
Following a struggle, Kuol was fatally shot twice in the neck by Macumber.
What Macumber didn't know when he set out alone that night was that another police officer was attacked months earlier at that same address, the judge noted.
"There was information available on the (system) regarding Mr. Fermino and the location which could have altered the course of events," reads the report.
A fifth recommendation stresses the need for CPS to review its two-officer unit policy.

Beaton said the policy has been updated since Kuol's death. He said there are still situations, day or night, when it is not worth sending two officers to a scene. Police will review the "grey area" around those calls that have the potential to become violent, but historically don't, he said.

"This was a 'check on welfare' call," said Beaton. "(Macumber) expected to find someone drunk and passed out in a hallway. When he got there, things changed quickly. Our officer reacted with the training we gave him."
Calgary Police Association president Al Koenig said one-officer units respond to calls overnight "on a regular basis."
"It happens too often," Koenig said. "One of these times we are going to have another fatality."
George Blochert, the lawyer for the Kuol family during the fatality inquiry, said he likes the recommendations, but added it's impossible to say if implemented they'll prevent another death.

"The reality is you can have another situation with a slightly different set of circumstances and have another death," said Blochert. "But these were good recommendations appropriate to the goal of the fatality inquiry of trying to prevent this sort of thing from happening again."
In the report, Meagher determined the officer's use of force was necessary, as did an internal investigation.
Macumber, who is on paid leave, declined comment Tuesday when reached at his southwest home.
Tut Kueth of the Alberta New Sudan Community Association said the recommendations are fine, but he still feels Macumber should have been charged.
"We're upset over this. It's not just Sudanese, all Calgarians should be upset," said Kueth.
Macumber has been involved in two other controversial shootings since the fatal incident.

In March 2005 he was charged with common assault, careless use of a firearm and two counts of unauthorized possession of a firearm after a shot was fired in his home Dec. 28, 2004. That incident, Beaton said Tuesday, is still under investigation.
Last June, Macumber made headlines again when he shot a dog while investigating a car prowling complaint.
Koenig said the Kuol incident has taken an "enormous emotional toll" on Macumber.
